extracted.intended_audience: employers, workers, labor lawyers, HR professionals, and DOL enforcement staff
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory guidance for determining whether a worker is an employee or an independent contractor under the FLSA using an economic-reality, multifactor test—with emphasis here on the skill-and-initiative factor and the scope/limits of catch-all additional factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skill and Initiative factor (§ 795.110(b)(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the worker brings specialized skills to the work relationship, this fact is not itself indicative of independent contractor status because both employees and independent contractors may be skilled workers. It is the worker's use of those specialized skills in connection with business-like initiative that indicates that the worker is an independent contractor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department explains that the factor asks not merely whether a worker is skilled but whether the worker uses specialized skills in a business-like way (e.g., marketing skills, obtaining work from multiple clients, exercising independent business judgment) to show they are in business for themselves. The rule recognizes case law (e.g., drivers, unloaders) and clarifies that certain occupations often lack specialized skills but are not predetermined to be employees. Examples: a highly skilled welder who makes no independent business decisions and is told what to do indicates employee status; a specialty welder who markets services to multiple companies and obtains work indicates independent contractor status. The Department clarifies that a commercial driver's license (CDL) can indicate specialized skill, but it is the use of that skill in connection with business-like initiative that matters. The Department also notes that this factor may point to employee status where the work is dependent on training from the employer to perform the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence on employer-provided training
rubrics_metrics.description: If the work is dependent on training from the employer to perform the work, that dependence indicates employee status under the skill-and-initiative factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all employer-paid or employer-arranged training negates independent-contractor status (e.g., paying for a first-aid class does not necessarily make a contractor an employee). The analysis focuses on whether the worker is dependent on the employer's training to perform the work in question. The Department emphasizes totality of circumstances rather than isolated trainings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional factors (§ 795.110(b)(7))
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional factors may be relevant in determining whether the worker is an employee or independent contractor for purposes of the FLSA if the factors in some way indicate whether the worker is in business for themself, as opposed to being economically dependent on the employer for work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a constrained catch-all: only factors that indicate economic dependence or independence should be considered. The Department retains the provision without listing particular additional factors, explaining courts and prior DOL guidance long have treated enumerated factors as non-exhaustive. Commenters urged deletion or specification; the Department declined, noting that the regulatory language limits scope by requiring relevance to economic dependence. Examples of potential additional factors suggested by commenters include recognized treatment under other statutes, business formalization (incorporation/licenses/taxes), transparency of contracting terms, and written agreements—but the Department warns these may be mere labels and should be evaluated for whether they reflect economic reality. Additional factors may often be unnecessary because relevant facts can be assessed under the enumerated factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality-of-the-circumstances / No predetermined weight
rubrics_metrics.description: The determination of employee vs. independent contractor must be grounded in the economic reality of the whole activity and determined by reference to the totality of the circumstances; no single factor is controlling and no predetermined immutable weights should be assigned to particular factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department cites Silk and decades of case law to support the non-mechanical application of the factors. The rule rejects commenters' proposals to elevate or consistently weigh certain factors above others (e.g., by assigning core vs. non-core status or fixed weights), explaining that doing so would ignore the fact-specific nature of the inquiry across occupations and time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business formalization and documentary labels are not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts such as whether a worker has incorporated, holds a business license, receives an IRS Form 1099, or signs a contract indicating independent-contractor status may reflect labels rather than economic realities and are not automatically determinative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department cautions that incorporation, 1099 forms, business licenses, and contractual provisions can be considered only to the extent they actually evidence that the worker is in business for themself as a matter of economic reality. Such facts may be considered either as additional factors or under enumerated factors to which they are relevant, but they are not by themselves dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlap among factors is permissible
rubrics_metrics.description: Some facts showing an exercise of initiative may be considered under more than one factor (e.g., skill-and-initiative and opportunity for profit or loss based on managerial skill) if appropriate depending on the facts of a case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department explains that considering the same facts under multiple factors is consistent with and furthers the totality-of-the-circumstances approach. The rule does not forbid overlap; rather it acknowledges that certain instances of initiative are probative under multiple factors and that the ultimate determination depends on all factors together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declination to adopt 'degree of independent business organization and operation' as a standalone factor
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declines to identify the 'degree of independent business organization and operation' as a separate, standalone seventh factor in the analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning: the Department is unaware of any court that has used this as a standalone factor; elements like incorporation or receipt of 1099s may be mere labels rather than indications of economic reality. The Department will instead allow relevant considerations about business organization to be evaluated under the additional-factors provision or under enumerated factors as appropriate.
